sec.title: Background and aim
sec.p: Despite progress in traditional treatment methods, the overall survival rate for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains limited. Consequently, it is essential to investigate alternative therapeutic strategies to enhance patient outcomes. This review highlights the potential role of plant extracts as chemo preventive agents in oral cancer treatment.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines, involving an extensive literature search from databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of science, Cochrane and CINAHL which included studies from 2010 to 2024 that explored the anticancer potential of medicinal plants for OSCC treatment. Data extraction focused on plant species, parts used, extract type, active components, dosage, and cancer cell lines or animal models used. Risk of bias was assessed using the OHAT tool for animal studies and the ROBINS-I tool for in vitro studies.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 12 in vitro and animal studies were included, examining plants such as Allium sativum (garlic), Crocus sativus (saffron), Curcuma longa (turmeric), Scutellariabaicalensis (Baikal skullcap), etc., These studies demonstrated that bioactive components like allicin, curcumin, and baicalin significantly inhibited OSCC cell proliferation and induced apoptosis. However, there was substantial variability in the dose concentrations required, ranging from 1 µg/mL for garlic extract to 50 mg/mL for saffron nanoparticles. The risk of bias assessment indicated that four studies had a moderate risk, while one had a low risk of bias, indicating methodological rigor.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Plant extracts such as Curcuma longa and Vitis vinifera present a promising, less toxic alternative for OSCC treatment, with the potential to be integrated into conventional chemotherapeutic regimens. While in-vitro and animal studies are encouraging, further clinical trials among humans are necessary to confirm their efficacy and safety in clinical settings.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: OSCC is the seventh most prevalent cancer worldwide, constituting about 4.5% of all cancer diagnosis globally and is often associated with poor prognosis and high mortality rate [1]. It leads to around 4,50,000 deaths annually, representing approximately 4.6% of global cancer-related deaths. OSCC is more prevalent in men than in women, and is more common in adults over 50 years of age [2]. While conventional treatment modalities such as surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy are effective, they are often accompanied by significant side effects and potential for recurrence. This has led to increasing interest in chemoprevention, particularly the use of dietary factors and plant extracts, as an adjunct to traditional treatments for OSCC [3].

Plant extracts have been used for centuries in traditional medicine and are now gaining recognition in modern oncology as viable alternatives or complements to synthetic chemotherapeutic agents. Their unique benefits stem from their natural origin, bioactive complexity, and reduced adverse effects. Unlike synthetic chemotherapeutic agents that indiscriminately target both cancerous and healthy cells, many plant extracts, such as Curcuma longa and Vitis vinifera show selective cytotoxicity toward cancer cells. This reduces damage to normal tissues, minimizing adverse effects such as nausea, fatigue, and immunosuppression associated with drugs like cisplatin. Natural compounds are often biocompatible and better tolerated by the human body, leading to lower systemic toxicity. Plant-based drugs can be cultivated and extracted at a lower cost compared to the high expenses of synthesizing and developing synthetic drugs in laboratories which makes them a more affordable option, particularly in resource-limited settings.

Dietary components, such as polyphenols, flavonoids, and carotenoids found in fruits, vegetables, and plant-based supplements, have shown promise in preventing cancer development by neutralizing oxidative stress, reducing inflammation, and inhibiting cancer cell proliferation [4]. For instance, curcumin from turmeric, green tea polyphenols, and resveratrol from grapes are well-documented for their anti-carcinogenic properties. These compounds act by modulating key molecular pathways such as NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and PI3K/AKT, which are involved in cancer cell survival and metastasis [5, 6].

Medicinal plants have been used for centuries in traditional medicine systems across the globe, and their potential as anticancer agents has gained increasing attention in modern scientific research. The bioactive compounds found in these plants, such as alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids, and phenolics, exhibit a wide range of therapeutic properties, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer activities [7–9]. These natural compounds can influence cancer development by inducing apoptosis, inhibiting cell proliferation, and modulating molecular pathways involved in tumor growth and metastasis [10].

Many medicinal plants act as natural antioxidants, helping to neutralize free radicals that can cause DNA damage and promote carcinogenesis. For instance, compounds such as curcumin from Curcuma longa (turmeric), resveratrol from Vitis vinifera (grapes), and catechins from Camellia sinensis (green tea) are potent antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and inflammation which are key factors in cancer development. Regular consumption of these plants as part of a balanced diet has been linked to a lower risk of certain cancers, including colorectal, breast, and prostate cancers [11–14].

Chemoprevention refers to the use of natural or synthetic substances to prevent, halt, or reverse the development of cancer. Medicinal plants are rich sources of chemopreventive agents that can inhibit cancer cell growth, promote apoptosis, and suppress angiogenesis [15]. For example, sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, has been shown to block tumor growth by inhibiting histone deacetylase (HDAC) enzymes, which play a role in cancer cell proliferation [16]. Studies have also highlighted the potential of other plants such as Moringa oleifera, Withaniasomnifera (ashwagandha), and Catharanthus roseus (Madagascar periwinkle), whose extracts contain compounds that can target specific cancer pathways, reduce tumor size, and enhance the effectiveness of traditional chemotherapy treatments. These plants offer a complementary approach that can reduce the toxic side effects of conventional therapies while improving patient outcomes [17, 18].

Given the increasing concerns about the side effects of conventional cancer treatments like chemotherapy and radiation, medicinal plants offer a promising complementary approach. Their natural bioactive compounds could enhance the efficacy of existing therapies while minimizing adverse effects, making them an attractive option for integrative cancer treatment strategies. As the exploration of plant-derived anticancer agents continues, ongoing research is crucial for identifying and developing novel compounds with potent anticancer effects [19, 20].

sec.title: Study protocol
sec.p: The Systematic review adhered to the guidelines set forth by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) for the selection of studies, synthesis of data, and eventual dissemination of results [21].

sec.title: Information sources and literature search strategies
sec.p: A comprehensive search was conducted on PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of science, Cochrane and CINAHL to find research papers published from January 2010 to October 2024 that analysed several medicinal plants for their anticancer potential and chemotherapeutic properties. The MeSH combinations includes “Medicinal plants OR bioactive plants OR potential medicinal plants” AND “anticancer activity OR anticancer property OR anticancer methods OR pharmacological activity OR in vivo activity OR in vitro activity AND chemotherapeutic property”. These keywords were categorized into three groups, and a comprehensive exploration of all conceivable combinations among the terms in these three groups was conducted. The articles were filtered based on the availability of full-text, quality of the published paper and the amount of bias. The search identified in-vitro and animal studies but not randomised controlled trials. The identified articles were then imported into Mendeley Desktop 1.13.3 software (Mendeley Ltd, London, England) to identify and eliminate duplicates.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The study selection was based on the following inclusion and exclusion criteria.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p:
Inclusion criteria.
Studies should include medicinal plants with anticancer potential
Studies should include medicinal plants used for chemoprevention
Review articles are included
Animal and in-vitro studies
Studies published only in English language

Exclusion criteria.
Case reports and case series
Studies about medicinal plants with other properties All relevant text, tables, and figures were examined during data extraction, and discrepancies between the two authors were resolved by discussion or consensus. The third reviewer resolved any disagreements occurred between the two reviewers.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: A systemised data extraction technique was incorporated for extracting data that includes study title, first author, journal, year of publication, place of study, study design, medicinal plants, anticancer property, chemotherapeutic property.

sec.title: Risk of bias analysis
sec.p: To assess the risk of bias of included studies, Oral Health Assessment Tool (OHAT) [22] for animal studies, and ROBINS-I tool for in-vitro studies was used [23]. Risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers for all the studies included and discrepancies were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer. The domains for risk of bias assessment were based on Randomization, Allocation Concealment, Comparison group, Confounding, Experimental conditions, Blinding, Complete outcome data, Exposure Characterization, Outcome Assessment, Outcome Reporting and No other threats.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p:
The initial search resulted in 261 studies, Out of which 73 full-texts articles were selected for the review process. The final synthesis yielded 12 studies after excluding articles which were narrative reviews, case reports and systematic reviews which were included in the current review [Fig. 1].Fig. 1
PRISMA flowchart identifying studies via databases and other methods

sec.p:

sec.title: Outcome assessment
sec.p:
The 12 medicinal plants were assessed for anticancer potential and each extract exhibited varying degrees of cytotoxicity, apoptotic induction, or inhibition of carcinogenesis. In vitro studies showed that compounds like allicin (Allium sativum), crocetin (Crocus sativus), and curcumin (Curcuma longa L) effectively inhibited OSCC cell growth and modulated pathways involved in cancer progression. The combination of Curcuma longa L with cisplatin has shown enhanced anticancer activity and reduced drug resistance [24]. Unlike synthetic chemotherapeutics, these plant compounds act on multiple cancer pathways, reducing the likelihood of resistance [24–26]. Similarly, in vivo animal studies demonstrated promising results, such as the reduction of DMBA-induced buccal pouch carcinoma in hamsters using Ocimum sanctum and anti-carcinogenic effects from Zingiber officinale’s active compound, shogaol [35, 36]. While the extracts exhibited anticancer activity, the differences in dose, extract type, and cell lines used emphasize the need for standardization to assess their therapeutic applicability comprehensively [Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 2]. These plant extracts inhibit carcinogen activation and enhance DNA repair mechanisms, thereby reducing the risk of cancer in high-risk population. They offer a multitargeted approach to oral cancer prevention and treatment, addressing tumor growth, metastasis, and inflammation while reducing treatment-associated toxicities. sec.p:

Twelve studies were used for the bias assessment [24–35], out of which four showed a moderate risk of bias and one showed a low risk of bias across all the domains, implying strong methodological outcomes and reporting. Moderate and low risk of bias in the included studies denoted that they have robust methodologies, with minimal threats to internal validity. This ensures that the reported results of five studies are more likely to reflect true effects rather than systematic errors; whereas seven studies with critical risk of bias typically compromised on the overall reliability and affects the certainty of anticancer findings.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The present study examines 12 various plant-based compounds tested in vitro and through animal models for their potential anticancer properties, particularly targeting oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Numerous plant species, including Allium sativum (garlic), Crocus sativus (saffron), and Curcuma longa (turmeric), have been explored due to their bioactive components and potential therapeutic applications. [24, 26, 36]. The study’s results suggest that natural plant-derived compounds can exhibit cytotoxic effects against cancer cell lines or mitigate carcinogenic processes in animal models. However, the specific mechanisms of action and clinical efficacy of these compounds require further elucidation.

Each plant extract tested reveals a unique set of bioactive compounds with potential anticancer effects. For example, Allium sativum (garlic) contains allicin and flavonoids, which demonstrate cytotoxicity in OSCC KB cells at a low dose (1 μg/mL). Similarly, Crocus sativus (saffron) contains crocetin and safranal, which have been evaluated in nanoparticle form for their cytotoxic effects on OSCC cell lines at a much higher dose (50 mg/mL). The diversity in concentration levels and chemical profiles suggests that plants offer a broad range of potential anticancer agents, albeit with varying potencies [24, 25, 37].

The study features both in vitro and in vivo approaches to understanding plant-based compounds. For instance, while Allium sativum, Crocussativus and Vitis vinifera were tested in vitro on OSCC cell lines, Dracaena cinnabari (Dragon blood tree) and Ocimum sanctum (Holy Basil) were tested in animal models. Allium sativum, Crocus sativus and Vitis vinifera modulates the p53 pathway, inhibits angiogenesis by reducing VEGF levels, and induces apoptosis by targeting Bcl-2 proteins [24, 25, 32]. Dracaena cinnabari showed potential efficacy at 1000 mg/kg in rats and the extracts may suppress metastasis by inhibiting pathways such as the PI3K/AKT pathway and related gene targets, which are crucial for cancer cell survival and migration, while Ocimum sanctum demonstrated chemopreventive effects in DMBA-induced buccal pouch carcinoma in hamsters as they stabilize mast cells, suppress IgE, and inhibit the release of inflammatory mediators, contributing to its anticancer potential [28, 33, 38]. These examples underscore the necessity of different experimental approaches to assess both cellular-level effects and overall physiological responses.

A critical observation across the study is the significant variation in the dose concentrations required to exhibit anticancer effects. While certain compounds, such as the aqueous extract of Allium sativum, are effective at low doses (1 μg/mL), others, like the saffron nanoparticles from Crocus sativus, require substantially higher concentrations (50 mg/mL) for similar in vitro efficacy [24, 26, 37]. This variability may reflect differences in compound stability, bioavailability, or cellular uptake mechanisms, highlighting the need for standardization and optimization in future research.

Although the study provides a broad overview of various plants and their anticancer potential, it does not delve deeply into the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects. For instance, Curcuma longa (turmeric) has been recognized for its ability to inhibit epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in human gingival fibroblasts (HGF), a key process in cancer metastasis. It also inhibits NF-κB, COX-2, and STAT3 pathways simultaneously, reduces oxidative stress, induces apoptosis via mitochondrial disruption and caspase activation, and prevents angiogenesis [25]. Further exploration into how these bioactive compounds modulate molecular pathways, such as apoptosis, cell cycle regulation, and metastasis inhibition, will be crucial for advancing these compounds towards clinical applications.

Despite the promising in vitro and animal model results, the leap to clinical application remains a significant challenge. Factors such as bioavailability, systemic toxicity, and the pharmacokinetics of plant-based compounds require thorough investigation. Additionally, the safety profiles of high-dose extracts like saffron nanoparticles or the methanolic resin extract of Dracaena cinnabari need to be carefully evaluated in the context of human use [34]. Nonetheless, the findings suggest that with appropriate formulation and delivery mechanisms, these compounds could serve as adjunct therapies in cancer treatment [39].

Future research should focus on standardizing extraction methods and identifying the most potent bioactive compounds within each plant species. Clinical trials assessing the efficacy and safety of these compounds in humans are also warranted, especially for compounds that show significant promise in preclinical models, such as curcumin from Curcuma longa and baicalin from Scutellariabaicalensis by activating caspase-3 and caspase-9, critical mediators of apoptosis. They also inhibit the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which is often hyperactivated in cancers, promoting cell survival and proliferation [26, 36]. The exploration of plant extracts as chemotherapeutic agents offers a natural, less toxic approach to OSCC treatment. By targeting key molecular pathways involved in cancer development, these bioactive compounds could enhance the efficacy of conventional treatments while minimizing adverse effects [40]. However, further clinical studies are necessary to fully establish their role in OSCC therapy and to determine optimal dosing, safety, and efficacy. Exploring synergistic effects between plant-derived compounds and existing chemotherapeutic agents could open new avenues for integrative cancer therapies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Plant extracts present a promising avenue for the development of less toxic, natural alternatives or adjuncts to conventional chemotherapeutic treatments for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Their ability to target cancer-specific pathways, reduce inflammation, and induce apoptosis without causing severe side effects makes them ideal candidates for integrative cancer therapies. Comprehensive dose–response studies are needed to identify the optimal therapeutic concentrations of bioactive compounds. This will help bridge the gap between preclinical and clinical applications. However, despite encouraging preclinical data, extensive clinical studies are still required for specific compounds with strong preclinical evidence, such as Curcuma longa L, Vitis vinifera, and Scutellariabaicalensis, should be prioritized for RCTS to confirm their efficacy, determine appropriate dosing, and assess their safety in a clinical setting. Future studies should prioritize the use of standardized extraction and purification protocols to ensure consistency in the composition of plant extracts. International guidelines, such as those from the WHO or ISO, can be adopted to achieve this.
